extracted.intended_audience: users of Singular (mathematicians, researchers, and students doing computational algebra / singularity computations)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and examples for performing elimination, free resolutions, graded-module handling, Ext, factorization, primary decomposition, normalization, kernel computations, algebraic dependence tests, and singularity invariants in the computer algebra system Singular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of eliminate vs. standard-basis elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: In Singular the most convenient way is to use the eliminate command. In contrast to the first method, with eliminate the result needs not be a standard basis in the given ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There may be cases where the first method (producing a standard basis) is preferred. For local or mixed orderings elimination needs special care: eliminate computes the closure of the image of V(J) under projection pr : k^r × (k^n,0) → (k^n,0) (so components meeting fibers outside the origin are included). Achieve this by using an ordering where the block of t-variables has a global ordering (preceding the x-variables) and the x-variables have a local ordering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling weighted-homogeneous (quasihomogeneous) input
rubrics_metrics.description: If the input is weighted homogeneous (=quasihomogeneous), the weights given to the variables should be chosen accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singular offers function weight which proposes integer weights so the ideal/module is as homogeneous as possible (works if input is weighted homogeneous but may be slow for many variables). Use qhweight to check quasihomogeneity: it returns an intvec of correct weights if input is quasihomogeneous and an intvec of zeros otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing free resolution command based on input and goal
rubrics_metrics.description: Several commands compute free resolutions, each with different methods and input requirements (res, fres, lres, mres, sres, nres, minres, syz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: res: heuristic preferred method. fres/sres: use Schreyer’s method; input must be a standard basis. lres: LaScala’s method; input must be homogeneous. mres: minimal free resolution via syzygy method. nres: standard-basis method. minres: minimizes a free resolution. syz: computes first syzygy module. Use res(i,r), lres(i,r), sres(i,r), mres(i,r), nres(i,r) to compute first r modules (r=0 for full resolution if basering not qring). Note: betti does not require a minimal resolution for minimal Betti numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution object structure and conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A free resolution in Singular has type resolution, storing all information related to free resolutions; conversion to type list yields a list of modules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The k-th module in the converted list is the first syzygy-module of the (k-1)-st module. Use list conversion to inspect modules, syzygies, and differentials; many commands (e.g., minor, reduce, size) can be used to verify relations between ideals obtained from resolution matrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing Hilbert–Burch situation via minors
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ideal i of a reduced curve in K^3, Hilbert–Burch theorem: i has a free resolution of length 2 and i is given by the 2x2 minors of the second matrix in the resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute resolution (e.g., mres), extract the appropriate syzygy matrix (resi[2]), take its 2x2 minors, and check containment via reduce/std to verify equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting generators not containing certain variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the proc 'nselect' from elim.lib to select generators from a std-basis that do not contain specified variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical use: compute std basis j, then j = nselect(j,1..4) to select generators not containing variables 1..4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assigning and checking graded-structure of modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Check and assign homogeneity attributes for modules: attrib(I,"isHomog") and homog(I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: homog(I) assigns an admissible weight vector (example: 2,2,1,1,0) which becomes attribute 'isHomog' (accessible via attrib). Use betti(...,0) to infer degrees from Betti diagram; attrib does not get checked for admissibility by Singular; assigned attributes are lost under type conversion (e.g., module to matrix). You can shift degrees by attrib(J,"isHomog",DV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading degrees from Betti diagrams and rowShift attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree corresponding to the first non-zero row of the Betti diagram is accessible via the attribute 'rowShift' of the betti matrix (type intmat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute betti(res,0) or betti(I,0) and inspect attrib(betti(...)) and the matrix to get graded information and row shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing Ext groups via resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: To calculate the n-th Ext group of an ideal: calculate a (minimal) resolution at least up to length n, apply the Hom functor (transpose), calculate the (n)-th homology group (ker/im).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: compute resolution rs = mres(I,n+1); let tAn_1 = transpose(rs[n]); compute kernel via syz on appropriate transposed entry; image is generated by columns; compute quotient via modulo(ker, image). Example proc ext shows this sequence. The library homolog.lib provides more advanced procedures (e.g., Ext, Ext_R) and options to return SB and vector space bases when third argument given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of Ext1 and Ext2 in deformation theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Ext1(M,M) and Ext2(M,M) are the modules of infinitesimal deformations and of obstructions of M (analogous to T1 and T2 for singularities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Ext1 is finite-dimensional, semiuniversal deformations can be computed using Ext1, Ext2 and the cup product. Use specialized procedures (Ext, Ext_R) for faster computations in common cases like Ext^k(R/J,R) with J an ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing depth via Auslander–Buchsbaum and resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the resolution over the polynomial ring; by Auslander–Buchsbaum, depth = number of variables minus length of a minimal resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: build module of Kähler differentials D, compute sres/std and betti, then compute N - ncols(B) + 1 to get desired depth-related quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization libraries and output format
rubrics_metrics.description: Factorization uses C++ libraries Factory and libfac, and NTL for univariate factoring; factorize returns factors and multiplicities, first factor usually a constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavior depends on characteristic and extension fields: in char 2 or over algebraic extensions results differ (examples show factors and multiplicities). Use ring specifications (characteristic, extension) to control factoring domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary decomposition algorithms and returned format
rubrics_metrics.description: Two primary decomposition algorithms are provided: primdecGTZ (Gianni/Trager/Zacharias) and primdecSY (Shimoyama/Yokoyama).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both return a list of pairs of ideals where the second is the prime ideal and the first the corresponding primary ideal. primdecSY can produce embedded components; use minAssChar and radical to get minimal associated primes and the radical of the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding normalization output
rubrics_metrics.description: normal(I) computes normalization of a reduced ring R/I and returns a list of rings; ideals in these rings are named norid. The normalization of R/I is the product of factor rings of the list quotiented by norid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access rings via nor[1][i], setring to inspect norid and normap. For nor[2][i] let ci be its last generator; the integral closure of R/P_i is generated as R-submodule of total ring of fractions by 1/ci * nor[2][i]. Use setring/def to navigate returned rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing kernel of map into quotient via modulo
rubrics_metrics.description: For matrices A: R^r → R^m and B: R^s → R^m, modulo(A,B) = ker(R^r → R^m/Im(B)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The output is a module whose generating vectors span the kernel on the right-hand side. After computing C = modulo(A,B) one can verify A*matrix(C) lies in Im(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing algebraic dependence and subring membership via elimination/block ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Given g, f1,...,fr ∈ K[x1,..,xn], construct I = (Y1 - f1, ..., Yr - fr) ⊆ K[x,Xvars,Yvars]. Then I ∩ K[Y] are algebraic relations between f1,...,fr; g ∈ K[f1,...,fr] iff normal form of g w.r.t. I and block ordering X>Y is in K[Y].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provided procedure algebraicDep(J,g) implements this: if g==0 it eliminates to get relations; otherwise it reduces g modulo std(I) to check membership. Beware ring creation and restoration (Rhelp) and use imap to map objects between rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Milnor and Tjurina numbers: definitions and computation in Singular
rubrics_metrics.description: milnor(f) = dim_K(K[[x]]/jacob(f)), tjurina(f) = dim_K(K[[x]]/((f)+jacob(f))). tjurina(f) finite iff f has isolated singularity; milnor finite in char 0 under same condition. Singular displays -1 if dimension is infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute these via working in Loc(x)K[x] (ring with local monomial ordering such as ds, Ds, ls, ws, Ws). Use std/ vdim to get vector space dimensions; use option(prot) to shorten protocol during standard basis computation. Library sing.lib contains dedicated commands (see D.6.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical distinction between local (ds) and polynomial (dp) computations for critical points
rubrics_metrics.description: Using ds (local series ordering) computes Milnor/Tjurina numbers (local/germ information); using dp (polynomial ring) computes number of critical points in affine space (counted with multiplicity) and number of singular points of f on affine hypersurface f=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map polynomials between rings using imap or fetch. Compare vdim(std(j)) in dp vs ds to deduce counts: difference between vdim in polynomial ring and localized ring gives number of critical points away from origin, and equality vdim(std(j+f)) indicates smoothness outside origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computing polar curves via partial derivatives and saturation/ideal quotient
rubrics_metrics.description: Define polar curve for f(x,t) w.r.t t as Zariski closure of V(∂f/∂x1,...,∂f/∂xn) \ V(f) if it is a curve; some authors take V(∂f/∂xi) itself as polar curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute j = diff(f,x1),...,diff(f,xn). To remove branches contained in f=0 (set-theoretic polar curve) take ideal quotient q = quotient(j, ideal(f)) or saturation qsat = sat(j,f)[1] (for large k j:f^k). Use elim.lib for saturation and sing.lib for singular-locus queries; check q and qsat coincide by testing both reductions reduce(qsat, std(q)) and reduce(q, std(qsat)) equal zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imap and fetch for ring mappings
rubrics_metrics.description: imap is a convenient ringmap for inclusions and projections of rings; fetch works for almost identical rings (e.g., differing only in ordering or variable names) and may be used to rename variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imap to map objects defined in one ring to another ring with same variable names; fetch is suitable for nearly identical rings. Integers and strings are global and do not belong to any ring.
